title: PSA: Don't sleep on unit tests and end-to-end (e2e) tests
author: geddy
selftext:
It might be the most boring part of software development for some, but the importance cannot be overstated. Your code needs tests!

I recommend updating your agent config file (claude.md or whatever you use) and tell it, "whenever a file is touched, be sure to update relevant test suites. If a test suite does not exist for that file, create one. Before any merges to main, ask me if I'd like to run the full test suite."

For those non-devs, a unit test tests a unit of work. So, individual functions, making sure clicking a thing makes another thing happen, ensuring input to a function yields an expected output, that sort of thing. An end to end test runs the actual implementation without mocking out anything. If you're building an app, web-based or not, you want it to actually *run the app* and interact with it.

For anything web-based, I recommend having it write e2e tests in Playwright, running headless mode with GPU support enabled. For native builds, I have no idea what is used, because that isn't my area of expertise.

I have unit tests on a per-file level that run via Vitest, and e2e tests that run simulations via Playwright (a browser automator) to make sure that nothing has broken between code pushes.

Claude has caught *tons* of regressions (things breaking that previously worked) due to having nearly a thousand unit and e2e tests.

**Now, let me explain why it is particularly a great idea to let your agent write tests, even though it's costing you tokens:**

Writing a unit test means thinking about all of the possibilities that can happen, good and bad,  handling any problems, and then writing a test around that scenario to make sure every possibility is covered. This allows your agent to simulate all possibilities, thus "thinking" more deeply about *what could go wrong*. While having it update a test for FileA, it might say, "wait, I realized there may be a bug in FileZ, I should fix that and update the test". This happens to me more and more the larger my code base is becoming.

Yes, it costs tokens, and costs time waiting for tests to run, but bugs are the first thing to get noticed in any game.

**Add tests to your project!**

comments.author: Manifesto-Engine
comments.body: visual debugging/regression  via videos. after something gets done, I test, make a video, point out what in the video and the agent will see themselves what's wrong as well. visual regression tests have helped me a lot so far.

replies.author: geddy
replies.body: Haven't moved to using videos yet, but that's a great idea.

replies.author: fapfap_ahh
replies.body:
Next step for you should be a GPU render script & skill so it can render and view it without you needing to record anything initially, only for the final round of fixes ;)

Mighty savings on context, accurate, and gets you a human playable test that has minimal changes needed afterwards.

comments.author: fuddlesworth
comments.body:
All my projects feature scriptable headless testing mode with screen shot capture.

It's been an amazing tool for bugs and verificaiton.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body: I agree but also I read the screenshots in the testing scripts chews up a lot of tokens

replies.author: fuddlesworth
replies.body: It does, that's why you only do it for specific things.

comments.author: robhanz
comments.body: Also, make sure you have actual unit tests (pure logic, don't need to be run in the game/renderer, etc.) for as much of your code as possible.  This lets you have a very fast test suite which can be run all the time, and then use the end-to-end or manual testing when done with significant chunks (in the background if possible) to keep velocity up.
